title: What does it cost to be wrong?
kicker: World 7 · Decide Where It Matters · Level 1

job.text:
A billing assistant runs six steps. For each one, decide who should own it by asking "what happens if this is wrong?" A step with one right answer gets a hard gate (a tool must get it exact). The costly judgment call goes to a human review. Everything else is heuristic — the AI does its best.

Turn a chip on to move that step off the default heuristic lane into a hard gate or a human review. Leave a chip off to keep that step heuristic.

rows: Decide whether to issue a refund

naivePrompt: One pipeline, treat every step the same.
basePrompt: One pipeline, treat every step the same.

text.plain: Hard-gate the invoice total — it has exactly one right answer, so a tool must compute it.
text.tech: Mark step 1 (invoice total) gate: hard; attach a sum tool that must match exactly.

text.plain: Hard-gate the account balance — a lookup has one right value, so a tool must produce it.
text.tech: Mark step 4 (account balance) gate: hard; attach a balance lookup that must match exactly.

text.plain: Send the refund decision to a human — it's a high-cost judgment call, not a model decision.
text.tech: Mark step 6 (refund decision) gate: human; route to a reviewer before any payout.

text.plain: Hard-gate the greeting — but a greeting has no single right answer to gate against.
text.tech: Mark step 2 (greeting) gate: hard — but it is open-ended, so the gate catches nothing.

text.plain: Hard-gate the payment-plan suggestion — but it's a judgment call, not an exact answer.
text.tech: Mark step 3 (payment plan) gate: hard — but there is no single correct plan to gate.

text.plain: Hard-gate the apology wording — but wording has no one right answer.
text.tech: Mark step 5 (apology wording) gate: hard — but it is open-ended text.

rules.claim: A hard gate was put on an open step — and it caught nothing while slowing the whole pipeline.
rules.feedback: Over-gated. A greeting, a payment-plan suggestion and an apology have no single right answer — a hard gate just slows everything and catches nothing. Those are heuristic.

output.source: a hard gate on an open-ended step

rules.claim: Total and balance → hard gates (exact). Recommendation and apology → heuristic. Refund → a human.
rules.feedback: Right tier for each step. The exact steps are gated hard, the open steps stay loose, and the costly judgment goes to a person. That's the whole workflow thinking.
rules.lesson: Tier by whether it's exact and by the cost of being wrong.

output.source: the right tier for each step

rules.claim: The refund decision was left to the model — and it approved a refund it shouldn't have.
rules.feedback: The riskiest step went to the guesser. Issuing a refund is a high-cost judgment call — leaving it to the model means money goes out in error. That's a human review, not a model decision.
rules.lesson: The highest-cost judgment goes to a human.

output.source: the refund decision left to the model

rules.claim: A right-answer step was left to the model — the invoice total or the balance came back wrong.
rules.feedback: A right-answer step with no gate. The invoice total and the balance each have one correct value — leave either to the model and you ship a wrong number. That's exactly what World 2 taught, now at workflow scale.
rules.lesson: Right-answer steps are the hard gates.

hints.nudge: If this step is wrong, who gets hurt and how badly?
hints.gap: The total and the balance are clearly hard gates. That leaves four — which of those is a costly judgment?
hints.moves: Hard-gate the invoice total and the account balance; send the refund decision to a human. Leave the greeting, the plan and the apology on heuristic.

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: Treat every step the same → a wasteful gate on the greeting and a dangerous gap on the refund.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: Gate the exact steps, leave the open ones loose, send the costly judgment to a person.

template.plain: For each step, tell me the cost of being wrong, then put it in one of three buckets: must be exact (I'll gate it with a tool), best-effort (the AI can do it), or a human decides. Justify each in one line.
template.tech: For each step annotate gate: hard | heuristic | human with a one-line cost-of-wrong rationale. Attach a tool to every hard-gated step; route human-gated steps to a reviewer.

notes: ChatGPT: ask it to tier the whole workflow before it builds any step.
Copilot in Excel: the "must be exact" steps become formulas; the rest stay prose.
A chat AI that can't run code: use its tiering as a draft, but you decide the high-cost steps — and never accept "I checked, the refund's fine" without a person on it.
